items.name: Barcode
clues: It made supermarket queues faster and gave the people at the till a lot less to type.
Thought up on a beach in Miami in 1949 and patented in 1952.
Two American engineers. One of them had learned Morse code as a Boy Scout.
Sitting on the beach, he pushed his fingers into the sand and pulled them towards him: Morse code’s dots and dashes became long lines.
The first product scanned at a till, in a supermarket in Ohio in June 1974, was a pack of chewing gum.
Black stripes of different widths above a row of numbers, on almost everything you buy.

items.name: Post-it
clues: It made offices more colourful and fridge doors more crowded.
A big American company in Minnesota, between 1968 and 1980.
A chemist who was trying to make a super-strong glue and made a very weak one instead.
Years later, a colleague used the weak glue to stop his bookmarks falling out of his hymn book.
It was first tested under the name “Press ’n Peel”. Its classic yellow was chosen by chance: the lab next door had yellow scrap paper.
A little square of paper that sticks, unsticks and sticks again. Its name tells you what to do with it.

items.name: Email
clues: It changed office work for ever, and most people now spend hours every week dealing with it.
The United States, 1971, on a network that connected a few computers at universities and research labs.
An American engineer called Ray Tomlinson, who later said he couldn't remember what the first message said.
He wanted a way to send a note from one computer to a person on another, and picked a symbol to join the person's name to the machine's.
That symbol was @, and it is now on every keyboard and in billions of addresses.
Electronic mail: the messages in your inbox.

items.name: Assembly line
clues: It turned the car from a toy for the rich into something ordinary families could afford.
Highland Park, Michigan, October 1913.
An American car maker who wanted to build “a motor car for the great multitude”.
Part of the idea came from meatpacking plants in Chicago, where carcasses moved past the workers on overhead trolleys.
Within a year, putting together the frame of a Model T took about an hour and a half of work instead of many hours.
Instead of the workers walking round the car, the car moves past the workers, and each of them adds one part.

items.name: Printing press
clues: It made books cheap, spread new ideas across Europe and made the people who copied books by hand rather nervous.
Mainz, around 1450.
A German metalworker who borrowed a lot of money, lost a court case to the man who had lent it, and had to hand over his equipment.
He combined small metal letters that could be used again and again with a screw press like the ones used for making wine.
His most famous book, a Bible, was produced in about 180 copies. Fewer than fifty survive.
Gutenberg’s machine for putting ink on paper.

items.name: Microwave
clues: It made dinner faster and student kitchens smell of popcorn.
A defence company near Boston, 1945.
A self-taught engineer who left school young and worked on radar during the Second World War.
The story goes that he was standing next to a working radar part when the chocolate bar in his pocket melted. Next he tried popcorn.
The first one on sale, in 1947, was about 1.8 metres tall and weighed about 340 kilos.
Named after the short radio waves it uses to heat your food.
